text: `systemctl is-active webapp` says `active`, and `systemctl status webapp` shows a real, running PID -- systemd isn't lying about the unit being alive. But `curl --max-time 5 http://localhost:8080/` still times out. So "active" here does not mean "doing its job." Check who is actually holding the port: `sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8080`.

The PID holding port 8080 belongs to a *different* unit than `webapp.service` -- `ps -p <pid> -o unit=` (or `systemctl status <pid>`) traces it back to `webapp-canary.service`. That's an old canary-rollout agent that was supposed to be decommissioned after cutover but is still enabled and starts on every boot, winning the race for the port before the real app gets a chance.

Meanwhile `webapp.service` itself really is running (`systemctl status webapp` shows a live PID) -- its binary just detects the bind failure, logs it, and idles forever instead of crashing. Check its own log for confirmation: `sudo journalctl -u webapp -e` (or `sudo journalctl --flush` first if it looks empty) shows "bind() failed, port already in use." That's why systemd shows it as healthy: the process never exits.

Decommission the leftover unit properly -- stopping it alone isn't enough, since it'll just win the race again on the next restart: `sudo systemctl stop webapp-canary && sudo systemctl disable webapp-canary`. Then let the real app actually bind: `sudo systemctl restart webapp`. Re-test `curl http://localhost:8080/` and confirm with `sudo ss -tlnp` that the PID now belongs to `webapp.service`.
